title: Eligibility can expand while the application route still loses people
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office analysis of Pell Grant eligibility and FAFSA completion before and after FAFSA simplification

pell_eligible.value: 9.9 million students; about 6% or 570,000 more than prior year

maximum_award_eligible.unit: students eligible for maximum $7,395 Pell award

observations.method: GAO review of federal law, Education policies and guidance, aggregated Education financial-aid data, and interviews with Education officials and five student-aid organizations.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison does not follow the same students through aid receipt or college outcomes and cannot by itself isolate formula changes from rollout delays or changes in applicants.
observations.subgroup: Students applying for federal aid; results are also examined by household income, assets, other family members in college, race and ethnicity, homelessness, and foster-care status.
observations.counterinterpretation: More eligibility can reflect a real access improvement even if application completion fell; conversely, eligibility alone does not show that students received aid or enrolled.

observations.period: SY 2024-25 compared with SY 2023-24; selected subgroup findings

denominator.unit: GAO subgroup comparisons within Education aggregate data

income_distribution.value: much of the overall increase occurred among households earning $60,001-$125,000

other_family_member_college.value: Pell eligibility rose from 55% to 60%; maximum-award eligibility rose from 48% to 77%
other_family_member_college.unit: students with another family member in college

vulnerable_populations.value: more than 90% were Pell eligible; most eligible students also qualified for the maximum
vulnerable_populations.unit: students identified as homeless or in foster care

possible_loss.value: a family of four with another student in college and $95,000 income could lose eligibility under the new rules

observations.method: GAO analysis of Education eligibility calculations and subgroup tables.
observations.uncertainty: The subgroup patterns describe eligibility, not award receipt, enrollment, persistence, or educational attainment; the named family is an illustrative calculation rather than a population rate.
observations.subgroup: Households differentiated by income and number of family members in college, plus students in vulnerable populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: A redistribution in eligibility rules can still expand overall access while producing losses for particular household configurations.

boundary: This record measures FAFSA completion and aggregate Pell eligibility before and after simplification. It does not establish aid receipt, college enrollment, persistence, graduation, debt change, or a same-student outcome.
